written: 2026-11-24, after all five variants were built, recorded and gate-checked; criteria.json was frozen before the build (g5 added after the build at Zach's request, FRs unchanged)
boundary: Five single-file React Flow builds on the real generated graph.json (robot_sdk main, 13 packages, 29 types, 253 uses, links from each package's robot-sdk.toml) and the real pick-and-place run (simulated MuJoCo plant). Recorded from the running builds. Not wired: no deploy, nothing applied to the live site or gh-pages; the 2x and links fixtures are TEST data used only through ?graph=.
defaultWhy: Commit Dashboard leads at 92/100: it is the only direction where the graph shows the one thing graph.json adds beyond today's site (declared + verified coverage per package and type) on the first screen, with a calm verdict, the commit stamp and a directory card; Type Switchboard is 3 points behind, so the call is fragile.
decisionHinge: How much the landing page is for an outsider's first minute versus for Zach's own 'who uses this type, and is it declared?' question. Move 10 points from FR1 (relationships) to FR3 (first-minute understanding) and Commit Dashboard 90 and Layer Atlas 89 tie at the top while Type Switchboard drops to 85; leave weights as frozen and V5/V2 are co-leaders.

variants.name: Layer Atlas
variants.thesis: A classic scroll landing page whose hero is the layer stack itself, one foldable React Flow diagram; types, viewers, the run, agents and the skill follow further down.
variants.bestWhen: The visitor first needs 'what is robot-sdk and how is it layered': pitch, install and the stack land in one screen.
variants.losesWhen: The question is type-first at this density: the type lens is busy at 8 types and small with all 29.

variants.name: Type Switchboard
variants.thesis: The robot_msgs type is the front door: pick one and the page re-centres on who produces it, who consumes it and where in the code, because the type is the API.
variants.bestWhen: The visitor arrives with a question about one type; it is answered on landing and one click narrows it to file:line.
variants.losesWhen: The visitor wants the whole system first: the layer picture and the directory are a tab away and the pitch is one line.

variants.name: Canvas Map
variants.thesis: The whole site is one zoomable React Flow map: the pitch, packages, types, the run, the agents and the skill are regions, so every relationship is spatial.
variants.bestWhen: The visitor wants to see how everything connects in place, with layers and agents still visible around a lit type.
variants.losesWhen: The visitor wants to read: at map zoom (~0.5) cards, link chips and blurbs are 6-11 px until you zoom in.

variants.name: Catalog

variants.losesWhen: The visitor wants the big picture: the first screen is a table and the full graph sits behind a Table/Graph switch.

variants.name: Commit Dashboard
variants.thesis: The landing page is a dashboard of the SDK at this commit: what is in it, how much of its type use is declared and verified, what the agents score and what the last real run measured.
variants.bestWhen: The question is 'is the stack healthy right now, where are the gaps, and where do I go next?'
variants.losesWhen: A newcomer wants a story: the pitch is short, the map is dense until a type is focused, and its lower half is below the fold.
